concepts.title: General Term of an Arithmetic Progression
concepts.definition: An arithmetic progression steps along by one fixed amount called the common difference; the term sitting at position n equals the first term plus one difference for every step after the first.
concepts.key_idea: Count the jumps from the first term, then add one difference per jump.

concepts.title: Number of Terms of an AP
concepts.definition: Reversing the general term counts the membership of a finite progression: divide the distance from first term to last term by the common difference and add one for the starting term.
concepts.key_idea: The span divided by the step size counts the jumps; one more term sits at the start.

concepts.title: Sum of n Terms of an AP
concepts.definition: Adding the first n terms of an arithmetic progression amounts to n copies of the average term: pair the outer terms, or equivalently take half of n times twice the first term plus one difference per extra step.
concepts.key_idea: Average term times how many terms; pairing first with last gives the same total.

concepts.title: Arithmetic Mean and Inserting Means
concepts.definition: The arithmetic mean of two numbers is the value that would sit midway between them in a progression, namely their average; inserting k means between two endpoints splits the gap into k plus one equal jumps.
concepts.key_idea: One mean halves the interval; k means divide the gap into k + 1 equal steps.

concepts.title: Properties of an AP
concepts.definition: An arithmetic progression survives uniform edits: shifting every term by a constant keeps the difference, scaling every term multiplies the difference, every other term forms another progression, and three numbers sit in progression exactly when the middle one equals the average of its neighbours.
concepts.key_idea: Addition shifts nothing but values; multiplication rescales the common difference.

concepts.title: General Term of a GP
concepts.definition: A geometric progression grows by one fixed multiplier called the common ratio; the term at position n equals the first term times the ratio raised to one less than the position.
concepts.key_idea: Each position after the first adds one more factor of the ratio.

concepts.title: Sum of n Terms of a GP
concepts.definition: Adding the first n terms of a geometric progression uses the shift-and-subtract trick: multiplying the whole sum by the ratio and subtracting collapses the overlap, leaving a closed formula.
concepts.key_idea: For ratio 1 every term repeats and the sum collapses to n times the first term.

concepts.title: Geometric Mean
concepts.definition: The geometric mean of two positive numbers is the value that would sit between them in a geometric progression, obtained as the square root of their product; inserting k means splits the log-gap into equal ratio jumps.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply first, take the square root once; the mean is the middle term of three in GP.

concepts.title: AM-GM Inequality and Extremes
concepts.definition: For positive numbers the arithmetic mean never falls below the geometric mean, with equality only when all the numbers match; this pins down the least value of a sum with fixed product and the greatest value of a product with fixed sum.
concepts.key_idea: Equality forces the numbers equal, which is exactly where extremes occur.

concepts.title: Sum to Infinity of a GP
concepts.definition: When the ratio sits strictly between -1 and 1, later terms of a geometric progression shrink toward zero and the endless sum settles on the first term divided by one minus the ratio.
concepts.key_idea: Convergence needs the magnitude of r below one; the tail contributes nothing.

concepts.title: Growth, Decay and Depreciation Word Problems
concepts.definition: Quantities that change by a fixed percentage per period form a geometric progression; a growth rate turns into a ratio above one, a depreciation rate into a ratio below one, and the worth after some periods is the starting value times the ratio compounded.
concepts.key_idea: Convert the percentage to a multiplier once, then compound it per period.
